stories.headline: One dead, 30 missing after ferry sinks off Vanuatu
stories.deck: The vessel, MV Matui, had set sail on September 11 with more than 40 passengers and crew from the island of Santo to Ambae island in very rough seas, but did not arrive
stories.bodyText:
One person died and 30 are missing after a ferry sank off the coast of Vanuatu, the South Pacific nation's government said on Sunday (September 13, 2026).
The vessel, MV Matui, had set sail on Friday (September 11) with more than 40 passengers and crew from the island of Santo to Ambae island in very rough seas, but did not arrive.
"Our hearts and prayers are with the families who have lost loved ones. Search and rescue operations are continuing," read a statement from Vanuatu Prime Minister Jotham Napat's office on Sunday (September 13).
Fifteen of those onboard have been "accounted for alive" and one dead body has been recovered, the statement said.
"Over 30 people remain missing at sea," it said. An investigation into potential negligence has been launched.
"This loss appears to be the result of strong winds and marine warnings not being heeded, and possibly of negligence including overloading of the vessel," the statement added.
The Maritime Rescue Coordination Centre in Noumea, New Caledonia, said it is assisting with the search, and a French Armed Forces aircraft was deployed on Sunday (September 13) morning.
The centre said 12 people were located on Sunday morning.
The member of parliament for Luganville, Matai Seremaiah, who is assisting in the search, said efforts would concentrate on the southeast coast where currents may have carried survivors.

stories.headline: New No. 1 Elena Rybakina dethrones Aryna Sabalenka to win US Open title
stories.deck: Elena Rybakina triumphed at the US Open, claiming both the championship trophy and the prestigious world number one ranking. In a thrilling showdown against Aryna Sabalenka, Rybakina showcased exceptional skill and poise, winning her third Grand Slam and second major title of the year, while Sabalenka's remarkable run at Flushing Meadows came to an unexpected end.
stories.bodyText:
Elena Rybakina arrived in New York with the world No. 1 ranking already within reach. She left with something even bigger — the US Open trophy and a place at the summit of women's tennis.
Rybakina completed her coronation in emphatic fashion on Saturday, beating two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka 6-4, 5-7, 6-2 in the final at Arthur Ashe Stadium. The victory delivered the Kazakh her first US Open title, her third Grand Slam crown and her second major of the year.
The 27-year-old had already secured enough ranking points to replace Sabalenka at No. 1 next week simply by reaching the semifinals. But Rybakina refused to stop there, taking down the player who had ruled New York for the past two years and ending Sabalenka's remarkable winning streak at Flushing Meadows.
“It’s tough to find words right now, honestly,” Rybakina said after the win. “I don’t expect nothing like this coming to this tournament. I’ve been dealing with a little bit with an injury, but somehow everything aligned together on my side.”
The triumph also completed a remarkable hard-court double for Rybakina, who defeated Sabalenka in the Australian Open final earlier this year. 
She now needs only the French Open title to complete a career Grand Slam, having already won Wimbledon in 2022.
Rybakina keeps her cool as Sabalenka falters
The final had all the ingredients of another classic between the world's top two players, but Rybakina's trademark composure ultimately proved decisive.
The second seed immediately put pressure on Sabalenka's serve and created 12 break opportunities, converting three. Rybakina, the WTA Tour's leading ace hitter, struggled to find her usual rhythm on first serve, landing less than half of them in play, but compensated with relentless returning and clean ball-striking.
Sabalenka's frustration surfaced early. After double-faulting to hand Rybakina a 3-2 lead in the opening set, she smashed a ball into the stands and received a code violation. Rybakina then held her nerve to take the first set 6-4.
Sabalenka responded in the second, raising her aggression and finally finding a way through Rybakina's defences. After the Kazakh saved two break points while serving at 4-4, Sabalenka created another opportunity in the next game and this time converted it to level the match.
But Rybakina regained control in the deciding set. Despite showing a rare flash of frustration after missing a backhand on break point in the opening game, she quickly settled again and surged ahead 5-2 before closing out the biggest victory of her career in New York.
Sabalenka, who had been chasing a third consecutive US Open title, could only watch the opportunity disappear.
“I was just out there competing, trying to do my best with what I had there today,” Sabalenka said after the match. “Not good enough.”
Elena Rybakina holds the trophy after she won the women's singles final against Aryna Sabalenka. (AP Photo)
Sabalenka's New York reign ends
The defeat ended Sabalenka's 19-match winning streak at the US Open and denied her a place alongside Serena Williams and Chris Evert as a three-time consecutive champion in New York.
Sabalenka had dominated Arthur Ashe Stadium in recent years, reaching four straight US Open finals and at least the semifinals in six consecutive appearances. But Rybakina's combination of power, accuracy and remarkable calm proved too much.
Sabalenka herself acknowledged the danger posed by her opponent.
“Her serve is amazing, the way she's able to step in and overpower you on court, and especially if it’s a U.S. Open court where it’s super fast, it's definitely a huge advantage for her,” Sabalenka said. “A lot of things make her dangerous.”
The result also flipped the rankings at the top of women's tennis. Sabalenka had occupied No. 1 for 99 consecutive weeks, but Rybakina will officially take over the position on Monday.
For Rybakina, however, the biggest prize was the one she lifted at the end of the night. She earned $5.5 million — the largest prize in Grand Slam history — and turned a tournament that had once been a source of frustration into the scene of her greatest New York triumph.
“I honestly was coming here for the last 10 years, and it was never successful -- nothing close to that,” Rybakina said. “It’s just incredible. I’m falling in love with New York more and more.”

stories.headline: West Benagal govt. to revive Chandannagar’s French legacy
stories.bodyText:
Tourism Minister Shankar Ghosh announced that a ‘French festival’ will be organised in the city every year from now on to celebrate the India-France partnership
The West Bengal government has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with the French Embassy to restore Chandannagar’s colonial-era heritage and promote the town in Hooghly district as a major international tourism destination.
The project will begin with the renovation of the Registry Building, which used to be the main administrative office of the French rulers.
Chandannagar was once a French settlement. While the French left in 1950, the architectural heritage of the town continues to draw tourists. As part of a three-day celebration from September 11 to 13 to mark the initiative, a series of cultural programmes are being held across the riverbanks, with Tourism Minister Shankar Ghosh and French Ambassador to India Thierry Mathou attending the events.
“This town has several French structures. The city also housed several freedom fighters who revolted against the British. We have signed an MoU with the French Embassy in the presence of the Ambassador. Under this, we will restore the Registry Building and other French structures to preserve Chandannagar’s heritage,” Mr. Ghosh said.
The Minister also announced that a ‘French festival’ will be organised in the city every year from now on to celebrate the India-France partnership. “We have prepared a map for such heritage renovation projects- ‘Little Europe across the Ganges.” Chinsurah’s Dutch heritage, Srirampore’ Denis heritage, and Basnberiya’s Portuguese heritage will also be preserved in the same way. However, we are starting it from Chandernagore,” said Mr. Ghosh.
In 1696, the French East India Company opened their first trading post in Chandernagore after getting a permission from the Nawab Ibrahim Khan. Ten years later, they bought a larger area of lands in this town from Mughals and made it their permanent settlement.
There are several buildings in the town that are a reflection of rich architectural heritage of the town. Other than the buildings and structures that have been given the heritage tag, a total 99 Indo-French heritage structures have been identified (by the French) in Chandernagore that needs to be resorted.

briefs.headline: West Bengal professors oppose Govt.’s inter-university transfer Bill, call it an attack on education
briefs.deck: WBCUTA says arbitrary transfers will weaken universities already facing severe faculty shortages, vows to first write to the Governor, who is also the Cancellor of Universities, and make an appeal
briefs.bodyText:
The West Bengal College and University Teachers’ Association (WBCUTA) on Saturday (September 12, 2026) accused the State government of attacking education through its proposed teacher transfer Bill and said it would intensify its movement if the legislation was not withdrawn. The association said most of the higher education institutes already work with only 40-60% of their sanctioned teaching strength.
“This is a direct attack on the autonomy of universities. It will destroy the centres of excellence and ruin the academic atmosphere,” Jadavpur University (JU) professor Partha Pratim Roy said, a WBCUTA member, toldThe Hindu.
The W.B. Universities and Colleges (Administration and Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026 was tabled by Higher Education Minister Jagannath Chattopadhyay on September 10. The Bill states that employees, both teaching and non-teaching staff, can be transferred to any university and college across the State due to “administrative reasons” in consultation with the Chancellor and State government. There is no provision to take consent from the concerned employees.
“This is a direct attack on the autonomy of universities. It will destroy the centres of excellence and ruin the academic atmosphere. Brilliant students who are from economically backward will fall even further behind,” Jadavpur University (JU) professor Partha Pratim Roy and member of WBCUTA told The Hindu. He added that NAAC accreditation and NIRF rankings are also dependent on the teachers available at the institutes, without which the rankings will crash, rankings where JU has always remained at the top.
The teachers have vowed to first write to the Governor, who is also the Chancellor of universities. They will also hold a signature campaign, mass convention and a simultaneous protest march to make their voices heard. Despite these measures, if the government fails to roll back the bill even after these steps, the professors threatened that they would hit the streets. They will also take legal action against this bill after detailed consultation with legal experts.
Teachers have also pointed out transfer of a supervisor could lead to cancellation of the PhD registration of a student, as per University Grants Commission regulations. “Their years of work will go to waste,” said University of Calcutta professor Mahalaya Chattopadhyay.
When the Bill was tabled, Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari had taken multiple swipes at Jadavpur University and had said that “so-called pundits” would be sent to newly established institutions which would benefit from their experience.
A day before the Bill was tabled, in a march outside JU, Mr. Adhikari had said that they would restore “nationalism” on the campus and uproot all “anti-national” elements, for which they are “taking adequate measures” leading to concerns among professors about targeted transfers.
However, professors said that many of the new institutes where they are being threatened to get transferred to do not even have buildings or classrooms. They claimed that sending them there will only destroy the existing education system and do nothing for the new places.
“If they really wanted to change the situation, they would conduct new recruitment and give jobs to people which would also slowly help the new institutes grow, without destroying the existing academic system,” Subhoday Dasgupta, President of WBCUTA said.
“The language being used to threaten us has no place in a civilised society. How did the teachers who once taught these politicians also become their enemy?” Professor Gautam Maity, convenor of All Bengal University Teachers’ Association said. He also added that arbitary transfer is not the answer to better the education system, rather more fund allocation, rapid recruitments, and infrastructure development is the way forward.
“They are punishing teachers who dare to speak. But we have a responsibility towards the public, because these are public institutions, and we will not give up without a fight,” Professor Maity added.
Published - September 13, 2026 05:51 am IST

briefs.headline: Houthis say hit Saudi base after renewed fighting with Yemeni govt forces
briefs.deck: Late Sept. 12, Saudi authorities said a Houthi projectile fell in an area near the border, resulting "in two injuries and material damage to a mosque, several buildings, and vehicles"
briefs.bodyText:
Houthi fighters on Sunday (September 13, 2026) said they used drones and missiles to attack a military base in southern Saudi Arabia as renewed fighting with Yemen’s government forces forced growing numbers of civilians to flee.
The attack at the southern Sharurah base targeted “weapons depots and command and control centres that are managing the aggression against our nation and people”, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree wrote on X. The date of the operation was not specified. Clashes have increased this week between the Iran-allied Houthis and Yemeni government forces, which are backed by Riyadh.
On Saturday (September 12, 2026), the government forces said they had struck Houthi fighters in the Red Sea city of Mocha, and later attacked other Houthi positions in the southwestern part of the country. “Air Force of the Armed Forces targeted positions and barracks of the terrorist Houthi group with three airstrikes” in the Taiz region, the Yemeni military said on in a post on X.
U.S. news site Axios reported that Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman had twice called U.S. President Donald Trump to request American strikes on the Houthis last week but the request was rejected.
The ongoing clashes follow a week-long Houthi offensive that culminated in the group capturing the remainder of Yemen's Red Sea coast and several strategic islands, and cementing their hold on the Bab al-Mandab Strait at the sea's southern entrance.
The waterway has become an important artery for Saudi Arabian oil exports after Iran largely cut off shipments through the Gulf with its blockade on the Strait of Hormuz at the start of the war in West Asia. The Houthis have recently declared their own maritime blockade of Riyadh's Red Sea ports.
The government news agency Saba reported on Saturday (September 12, 2026) that Yemeni "forces destroyed vehicles and weapons and killed members of the Houthi terrorist militia" near the port of Mocha, and quoted a spokesman for the forces as saying they had also struck Houthi targets just outside the city.
The Houthis, meanwhile, said on Saturday evening (September 12, 2026) that over the past 48 hours, "Saudi enemy aircraft conducted 129 airstrikes" on areas under their control.
Yemen's civil war, which began in 2014 with the Houthi capture of the capital Sanaa, had been dormant since a ceasefire in 2022 but roared back to life in July.
Saudi Arabia first entered the war on the side of Yemen's internationally recognised government in 2015 and continues to support the Aden-based administration.
On Saturday night (September 12, 2026), Saudi authorities said a Houthi projectile fell in an area near the border, hours after issuing alerts warning of the risk of possible attacks. The civil defence directorate said the incident resulted "in two injuries and material damage to a mosque, several buildings, and vehicles".
'Not even a shelter'
The Yemeni civil war uprooted millions of people, and the latest fighting has led even more to flee their homes.
The fall of Mocha to the Houthis on Thursday (September 10, 2026) drove many residents to Aden, where the internationally recognised government is based.
One of the displaced, Abdulali al-Rajihi, said the Houthis "told us: 'Leave, scatter, you have half an hour'". "We fled wearing the clothes on our backs. And we took our children, as much as we could manage."
Saddam Ali escaped from Al-Waziyah with his 11 children and a few possessions crammed into a small pick-up truck. He said he hadn't found a single free house in the city, "not even a shelter".
The UN's migration agency said on Saturday (September 12, 2026) that, since July, 76,000 people had fled the fighting, a figure that had quadrupled since last week. It said it was providing support but warned that "needs are far outpacing what we can deliver".
"The situation is deteriorating by the day," it added.
The renewed fighting in Yemen has killed more than 500 people, according to sources on both sides.
Published - September 13, 2026 02:03 am IST

briefs.headline: How To Date A Fanatic: Politics of belonging
briefs.bodyText: In 2020, Aruni Kashyap’s short story How To Date A Hindu Fundamentalist was published in The Boston Review. I read it and found the story’s pulse invigorating. The story has now been published as a full-length novel with the same characters. How To Date A Fanatic is a political novel that vividly and hauntingly captures contemporary India, with an academic as its protagonist..It opens with an eerie scene of two friends, Rohit and Minti, running from goons in a dhaba and hiding in a water tank. Before they can think of anything else, the water level in the tank starts to rise..Set in post-2014 Delhi and its shared borders with Haryana’s hinterlands, the novel follows Rohit, a young assistant professor of English at Delhi University. He has returned from America with a PhD and lives near two childhood friends from Assam, Sarfaraz and Minti. Rohit is in love with Dhruv, a man younger than him. When Dhruv refuses to reciprocate, we follow a heartbroken Rohit as he navigates his desire and search for companionship through dalliances with several men. As Rohit’s life unfolds, with visits to parents back in Assam and parties with friends, the Indian state rearranges itself into a right-led, fascist regime. Aruni Kashyap takes us down the road with Rohit into an India that is changing universities, ‘modi’-fying ideas of religion, rights, reservation and freedom..From the outset, the author’s brilliance shines through. His writing has a poetic rhythm that builds into a canvas of the personal and political without jarring the prose. He exercises subtlety when required and then stuns the novel with strong details of changing Indian society. A soirée of academics at Minti’s apartment starts with light-hearted banter about their lives and contracts that bind them to the private university in Sonipat. We are let into the world of these academics not just through their material possessions but through their discussions of the current government and the larger politics of reservation in India. The conversation then slips into Rohit pining for Dhruv. Tackling scenes this way keeps the novel’s plot grounded while exploring broader concerns that continue to strengthen the core plot. I thought of Elizabeth Strout’s 2026 novel The Things We Never Say, and Kiran Desai’s The Loneliness of Sonia and Sunny, both of which handle this well. Indeed, Aruni offers a remarkable portrait of Indian queer political literary fiction through his writing..Urban-rural porosity.Unlike his debut The House with a Thousand Stories, which was largely set in rural Assam, this novel provides a view of the urban. In fact, it tackles both urban-rural borders and their porosity effectively. And this space has a lot to say in this novel..Traveling on One Leg: Hunt for selfhood amid daily chaos.Rohit belongs to a village in Assam. He manages to get an education in Delhi after school. He goes to America and returns to Delhi. He shuffles between Delhi, Assam, and Haryana’s hinterland where elite private universities are located. Throughout the novel, we listen to Rohit navigate these spaces and his identity in each of them. The author notices the nuances and makes the reader see them too through Rohit’s first-person voice. He is unhinged with his two friends, awkward at queer gatherings, doesn’t see the point in explaining to his parents about his singlehood and refusal of a heterosexual arrangement, and is politically uncaring about rising violence in ‘Mainland India’..Somewhere in the middle, he thinks to himself that he wants a comfortable life with certain luxuries he’s strived for: a sentiment hard to bypass after having lived in a village amid insurgency. Yet, as his closest friends change in the fight for a free nation, Rohit can scarcely push aside the discomfort growing around his life of stable luxury. The universities are changing, and so are the students and administration. Rohit can barely think of his life ever remaining the same. The claustrophobia is palpable throughout the novel. Alongside Rohit, it makes the reader think of getting out of the labyrinth with no end in sight..Masterful storytelling and rich analysis of what it means to be living under an oppressive regime in India make this a must-read. Between humour, satire, and heartbreak, Rohit’s story reaches the reader in beauty and sadness. Minti is a character who stays with the reader with many questions long after the novel has ended. Unlike Sarfaraz, who is largely elusive, it is her presence that adds more dimension both to Rohit’s life and the novel’s haunting plot. If we have a follow-up novel to this, let it be Minti telling us the story of an India in its ever-changing garb.

briefs.headline: Traveling on One Leg: Hunt for selfhood amid daily chaos
briefs.deck: Hunt for selfhood amid daily chaos
briefs.bodyText: If the feeling of loneliness while being surrounded by people could be bottled and sold, it would come in the form of Herta Müller’s Traveling on One Leg. The 2009 Nobel Prize-winning author depicts the main character, Irene, and her struggle to find herself. Semi-autobiographical, the novel explores three core themes of identity, exile, and isolation..In essence, it’s a novel that’s deeply personal to the author. Herta Müller is a Romanian-German novelist, poet and essayist, largely known for her work that showcases the dark realities of living under the Socialist Republic rule in Romania. In Traveling on One Leg, she digs into her own experiences to evoke a feeling of loneliness and disarray. It forces readers to experience some of the most undesirable situations alongside Irene..The Bare Bones Book Of Humour: A comic lens to perceive the world.Like Müller, Irene was born to a German family in Romania. In her later life, she moves to Germany hoping to find comfort away from authoritarian rule. There, she also explores a relationship with an emotionally unavailable man named Franz. Over the course of the novel, two other romances are teased, including one with Franz’s friend and stand-in Stefan, and Thomas, a bookseller constantly on the verge of an emotional breakdown. But Irene’s desperate pining to find belonging drives the narrative..It’s established early on that Irene is a product of Nicolae Ceausescu’s dictatorship, reflected in her struggle to develop an understanding of freedom and individuality. Escaping her home country is meant to open a door for liberty and autonomy, but she isn’t welcomed to a land of golden opportunity as she had hoped. Her interactions with officials bring back to the surface emotions that she tried to escape after leaving Romania..The experiences isolate Irene and force her to reexamine her understanding of what normal is..For many, these moments might not seem like much, but to others it’s a subtle and powerful nod to the pains of physical relocation. Despite being ethnically German and nationally Romanian, she feels no connection or kinship with either country. Leaving her home was supposed to be a relief, but instead it creates an invisible and unexpected hurdle in understanding who she is as an individual..Attempts to find identity.The men she meets in her journey are another failed attempt to find her identity. With Franz, it’s fast and exciting, but unstable and doesn’t last. Stefan is more reliable, but it quickly gets boring. Thomas pretends to understand the big picture, but like Irene, he doesn’t know who he is as an individual. Each has a list of qualities that, in a way, Irene is looking to adopt in herself. She has no real attraction to any of them as people, so she fruitlessly continues to entertain the idea of romance, flitting among the three of them with little direction or purpose..Much the same can be said for the structure of the book. The style Müller chose rewards the slower and more attentive readers who enjoy a lack of central plot and non-linear storytelling. A lot of time is spent detailing surroundings. Descriptions of animals chirping in the distance, long train journeys across Germany, architecture and room decor (or lack thereof) are all conduits to Irene’s struggle to find belonging..Water, mirrors and windows in particular are a recurring imagery, symbolising the unpredictable and transitional stage in her life. Irene’s journey doesn’t end satisfyingly, like most things both in life and in the novel. But then again, one has to ask oneself what satisfying means. At the start, Irene is able to leave an oppressive state alone, and as a woman, her character avoids being cornered into chasing marriage, childbirth or a career to feel fulfilled. She is messy and disorganised, allowing uncertainty and unpredictability to guide her even if it results in dead ends. Precisely why the novel can be both dissatisfying and enough, depending on what the reader is looking for.

stories.headline: Prakash Raj to visit 100 booths in Karnataka to bring evidence of arbitrariness, calls SIR a ‘scam’
stories.bodyText:
Calling the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) a “scam” and “conspiracy”, actor Prakash Raj said starting September 22 till September 30, he would visit 100 polling booths across Karnataka, and bring evidence on how arbitrarily the exercise has been conducted, which he said he would present as “National public hearing” at Jantar Mantar in Delhi on October 15.
Mr. Raj said he would also take “this fight” legally, after collecting all the evidence at different courts. He pointed out that at these polling booths, he, along with civil society groups, would do “social audit” by mapping the details, looking into each case of how and why the electors were put into the absent, shifted, duplicate, dead or others (ASDDO) list, and look into the enumeration forms of those who got notices to check if they filled them correctly, or even if not, what discrepancy the notice flags. Mr. Raj argued that these mistakes, for which people are queuing up, are not committed by the citizens who are being punished.
VIP treatment
Questioning the VIP treatment to prominent personalities like actor Shiva Rajkumar, the actor questioned if some people are “more equal”. Such people, who are in the Election Commission’s list of VIPs, where officials will come personally and clear the hearing process, should deny this treatment and stand with the public at this time, because this is outright bias against the common citizen.
“Does that mean just because you are popular, you get the privilege? And if you are not popular, if you are a common man, you are underprivileged in this country? Not fair.”
Criticising political parties across the board, he said, “From Rahul Gandhi to Narendra Modi, everyone offers biryani packets when it is about elections, but when it comes to situations where citizens need them, like now, in SIR, during Covid pandemic, they (political parties) leave the public on their own.”
“In a democracy, a voter decides who will govern, but this exercise is aiming to change that. With this, government wants to decide who can vote. Still no opposition party is speaking for their people who elected them,” he argued.
Forced incrimination
Further taking on the design of the exercise, Mr. Raj said the voters who have been deleted and put into the ASDDO list are told to get included through form-6, while the form-6 declaration itself says, “I am applying for inclusion in Electoral Roll for the ‘first time‘ and my name is not included in any Assembly constituency/Parliamentary constituency. I am aware that making the above statement or declaration in relation to this application which is false and which I know or believe to be false or do not believe to be true, is punishable under Section 31 of Representation of the People Act, 1950 (43 of 1950) with imprisonment for a term which may extend to one year or with fine or with both.”
This way, each voter who is seeking inclusion after being removed is “incriminating“ themselves. Does the Election Commission “technically and legally want each person to lie?” he questioned.
Against claims of inclusion
The actor further pointed to the immunity provided to the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners under Section 16 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023, which bars courts from entertaining or continuing civil or criminal proceedings against them for acts done or purported to be done in the discharge of their official duties. He said, “Such immunity is planned because they knew they are conspiring a scam, otherwise why else such clause be introduced just months before planning something like this?” he questioned, adding that if it was an inclusionary exercise, the timeline would have supported the claim and not been done in a rush.

stories.headline: SIR: While ‘VIP voters’ are protected from hassle, common man in Bengaluru has to run from pillar to post
stories.deck: For lakhs in Bengaluru, it is a struggle to even understand what they are expected to prove at the hearing centres, and what to do if they have no documents or have documents but are currently in another State
stories.bodyText:
Mohammed Sadiq, an auto driver, has seven members in his family, and all of them have received notices in the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. While four know when their hearings are scheduled, the other three notices have not yet reached the Booth Level Officers (BLOs).
With him being the only earner, and four members of his family having no documents except Aadhaar and ration cards, he wonders what will change after the hearing. While only half of the family can establish their eligibility as Indian citizens, he said they are worried about what will happen if they do not appear for the hearing as they have no documents.
A caste certificate, he said, costs ₹1,200 per person through agents, while his efforts to get one through the government portal have failed as his application has not progressed. “How can i afford to get one for so many people?” he questioned.
The office of the Chief Electoral Officer (CEO) has ensured that prominent persons will be added to the final rolls or will not be served notices as they are “VIP voters” and changes to their cases are being made through Form-8 and their names added to the final rolls from the convenience of their houses.
But for lakhs in the city like Sadiq, it is a struggle to even understand what they are expected to prove at the hearing centres, and what to do if they have no documents or have documents but are currently in another State.
While the hearing of SIR notices began on September 5, there has been no let-up in the chaos that has left voters running from pillar to post. Many citizens are saying that while BLOs and Assistant Electoral Registration Officers (AEROs) have been trying to help, the design of the system is such that they are also left with no option.
Progeny mapping cases
For instance, notices are issued under two categories — no mapping and logical discrepancy. In logical discrepancy cases, while a discrepancy related to the “self” only requires one document, discrepancies related to “progeny” require three documents — one of the elector (self), the other of the parent, and a third of the grandparent.
AEROs point out that many are struggling to produce even a document for themselves, while in several cases, the electors who received notices have lost their parents, or are over 80 years old, with practically no records to prove.
In such cases, AEROs were seen assisting voters, by even uploading documents that are not part of the indicative list, such as ration cards. In several instances at hearing venues in Chamrajpet, Frazer Town and Kalyan Nagar, AEROs uploaded the same ration card thrice — for the self, the parent, and the grandparent.
“The system is accepting the documents, but we don’t know what will happen in the final rolls,” an AERO said.
Pointing to another case, an AERO said that in a few instances, notices were issued to twins, seeking an explanation for “less than nine months of gap between the progeny”.
AEROs said they were clueless about how to prove such a situation, as birth certificates do not state that the children are twins and are issued separately in each child’s name.
In such cases, the government’s initiative to provide permanent residential certificates (PRCs) and caste certificates could have helped. However, many are not getting the certificates even when they apply in person, while applications submitted online are also not moving forward.

stories.headline: Rapido driver flees with passenger’s phone in Bengaluru, demands Rs 18k
stories.bodyText:
Chaithanya.Swamy@timesofindia.com

According to the complaint filed by Trideep Debnath, 25, a resident of a paying guest accommodation in BTM Layout 1st Stage, he had booked a Rapido two-wheeler ride from Narayanappa Garden 4th Cross to Marathahalli around 5.54am on Sept 6. Rapido rider 
Ashutosh Kumar
 arrived on a white scooter instead of the booked vehicle bearing registration number KA-01-HX-7232.

When they reached a fuel station in Madiwala, the driver stopped to get the air pressure checked for tyres. At that moment, when the victim got down from the scooter and was checking the backside tyre, the rider fled with the phone.

stories.headline: 4-day crackdown: 800 children rescued from 17k workplaces in Karnataka
stories.bodyText:
Bengaluru: A massive statewide crackdown on 
child labour
 has exposed a disturbing reality in 
Karnataka
 — nearly 800 children were found working in establishments ranging from hotels and eateries to garages and shops.
Police teams conducted raids at nearly 17,000 premises across the state following chief minister 
DK Shivakumar
’s directive to intensify the fight against child labour. The move came after Shivakumar reportedly witnessed a child labourer during his visit to Yeshwantpur APMC Yard in Bengaluru on Sept 8, prompting him to order a statewide crackdown.
Police launched the operation Wednesday across 962 police station limits, targeting commercial establishments, industries, hotels, shops, garages, eateries, roadside food stalls, milk parlours and other workplaces where children were suspected to be employed. Bengaluru emerged as the epicentre of the crackdown, accounting for 503 of the nearly 800 children rescued across the state. Vijayapura followed with 72 rescues, while 33 children were rescued in Tumakuru. In Bengaluru alone, police teams inspected 5,897 establishments under the jurisdiction of 188 police stations as part of the special drive.
The citywide operation saw 66 children rescued in the North division, 71 in East, 22 in Whitefield, 63 in Central, 54 in South, 84 in West, 17 in North-West, 14 in South-West, 55 in North-East, 13 in South-East and three in Electronics City.
Police said the children were being paid monthly wages ranging from Rs 10,000 to Rs 16,000. Many were employed in small establishments and informal businesses, highlighting the extent of child labour operating beyond the scrutiny of formal workplaces.
The rescued children included those from Karnataka as well as Bihar, Assam, West Bengal, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Jharkhand and Nepal, police said.
Police said the operation has also resulted in enforcement action against employers. FIRs have been registered in five cases against those accused of employing children, while multiple notices have been issued to employers in several other cases. Of the rescued children, 54 have so far been handed over to various district Child Welfare Committees (CWCs) for rehabilitation and care.
Poor economic conditions
The operation also laid bare the socio-economic hardships pushing children into the workforce. In several cases, parents or guardians were aware that the children were working.
“Illiteracy and poor economic conditions have forced these children to take up jobs. Along with rescuing them, we are counselling them to return to education. We are also speaking to their parents and guardians and advising them not to send the children back to work,” said a senior police officer involved in the statewide coordination of the drive.
Officials said the focus will now shift to preventing rescued children from returning to workplaces and ensuring they are brought back into the education and rehabilitation system.

briefs.headline: Bengaluru shifts to handmade eco-friendly Ganesha idols this festive season
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru
: The city is set to see more Ganesha idols made at sustainability-focused community workshops being used for celebrations during the festive season, as citizen groups, lake activists and resident welfare associations (RWAs) encourage families to move away from Plaster-of-Paris idols and embrace natural clay.
In the weeks leading up to 
Ganesh Chaturthi
, several neighbourhood groups across the city organised clay idol-making workshops, many of them free, giving children and families an opportunity to make idols using natural clay and mud. The idols made during these sessions will be placed in homes this weekend for the festival, which falls on Monday.
The workshops were an important part of the city’s efforts to make festive celebrations more sustainable. Organisers said the idea went beyond simply replacing PoP idols with clay ones: by making the idols themselves, participants, particularly children, gained a better understanding of the environmental impact of their festival choices. “Children are the best ambassadors of change. If they learn sustainable practices at a young age, they carry those values throughout their lives and influence their families as well,” said NH Subramanian, secretary of Benniganahalli Kere Community Development Trust.
Across Bengaluru, such workshops are increasingly becoming an annual feature of the festive calendar. HSR Citizen Forum, for instance, has been conducting clay idol-making sessions for more than a decade, helping hundreds of children learn about environmentally responsible celebrations.
For many families, the exercise has become a way of retaining the cultural and devotional significance of Ganesh Chaturthi. Stricter enforcement by civic authorities, along with years of awareness campaigns by environmental organisations, has encouraged more citizens to consider alternatives.
Organisers are also paying attention to the source of the clay used in these workshops, ensuring that it comes from authentic suppliers and remains completely biodegradable. This, according to them, has helped reassure families that their efforts towards sustainable celebrations do not come at the cost of tradition.

briefs.headline: Laboratory faces probe after surprise inspection in Bengaluru
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: A private environmental testing laboratory, Bengaluru Analytics and Research Laboratory Private Limited, has come under scrutiny after a surprise inspection by forest, ecology and environment minister Ramalinga Reddy and senior Karnataka State Pollution Control Board (KSPCB) officials found multiple irregularities.
The inspection found that the laboratory had obtained prior permission from the ministry of environment, forest and climate change (MoEFCC) stating that three analysts would be employed. However, only one analyst was present. Officials found that the other two had not worked at the laboratory for the past five months.
The laboratory’s Consent for Establishment issued by the KSPCB had also expired in 2025. Despite this, the unit was operating without a valid consent from the pollution control board.
Officials found that the laboratory lacked a proper system to dispose of waste generated from its activities. Instead, the waste was allegedly being discharged into an open pit.
The inspection has raised concerns over compliance with environmental regulations and the laboratory’s adherence to prescribed standards.

briefs.headline: Karnataka may bring back physical marks cards
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru: The higher education department is considering revoking its earlier circular on not issuing physical marks cards and only relying on digital ones.
At a meeting of vice-chancellors with higher education minister Basavaraj Rayareddi at Karnataka State Higher Education Council on Friday, VCs raised the issue of lack of physical marks cards.
At present, all academic documents are available only in digital format in the National Academic Depository-DigiLocker. NAD is a central govt initiative and acts as a 24x7 online storehouse of all academic awards such as certificates, diplomas, degrees, and marksheets, duly digitised. Credits are registered in the Academic Bank of Credits.
The 
University Grants Commission
 (UGC) had asked all higher educational institutions to use NAD services to verify academic records. The state govt, in the 2023-24 budget, decided to switch completely to digital marks cards following rampant issuance of fake ones. But the move caused inconvenience to students.
“We’ve been receiving requests from students and parents for physical marks. They’ve been complaining that digital marks cards are not accepted at many places, including some foreign universities and corporates,” said one vice-chancellor.
Another VC who attended the meeting said: “The minister understood the concern and responded positively. He said govt would fix the minimum and maximum rates at which marks cards are to be printed. There should not be any rate disparity between universities. It will also fix the quality requirements and safety standards necessary to prevent fake marks cards.”
Thulasi Maddineni, secretary to the higher education department, said: “We’re considering the VCs’ demand. We’re working on a system where both physical and digital marks cards can be used. Online verification is important to control fake marks cards. So, while physical marks cards will be issued, digital ones will also continue. In case anyone wants to verify the authenticity of a marks card, it will be available on 
DigiLocker
.”
At the meeting, it was also decided to constitute a committee to examine the basic infrastructure at universities that have not yet got National Assessment and Accreditation Council accreditation. The minister also instructed the VCs to take care of university lands and not tolerate land encroachment.
Also discussed was the compulsory introduction of geology as a subject in civil engineering. The VCs also discussed the introduction of job-oriented courses at both UG and PG level in aviation, railway engineering, and urban planning.

briefs.headline: Bengaluru police warn social media users against viral trend of 1980 avatars
briefs.bodyText:
Bengaluru
: Think twice before deciding to join the 1980 AI photo club, which is rapidly becoming a trend. Bengaluru police and cybersecurity experts have warned citizens that uploading high-quality selfies to unregulated, third-party apps secretly harvests sensitive biometric data and exposes users to massive 
identity theft
 risks. Some police stations in the city have already spread warning messages through posters and social media posts.
Speaking to 
TOI
, DCP (crime) Imam Raja Kasim said: “Miscreants use the AI-generated images of others displayed on social media as their DP, impersonating reputed person and luring unsuspecting victims into sharing personal or financial data. Sometimes even banking credentials can be obtained to siphon off funds from the account. 
Instagram
’s 1980s AI trends can also be misused to commit cybercrimes.”
Key cybersecurity & privacy risksBiometric data collection and facial recognition
: A clear selfie provides high-definition biometric data of your face. Once processed, this data can be used for facial recognition profiling or stored in training datasets without explicit future control
Deepfake and identity misuse
: High-quality original photos of your face are the ideal source material for malicious actors to create deepfakes. Uploaded photos can end up leaked, scraped, or traded on unauthorized networks, leading to impersonation, synthetic media scams, or identity theft
XIF and location metadata exposure
: Digital photos often contain hidden EXIF metadata, including your exact GPS location, device model, time, and date stamp. Uploading unedited original photos can inadvertently share where you live or work
Background data leakage
: Photos often capture sensitive details in the background — such as house numbers, vehicle licence plates, ID badges, family members, or children — exposing personal details to AI
How to protect yourself?Avoid unverified third-party apps
: Use reputable platforms rather than downloading unverified or pop-up mobile apps created specifically to capitalise on viral trends
Turn off AI model training
: Adjust app or platform privacy settings to opt out of data collection and model training
Strip metadata and crop
: Remove EXIF metadata and crop out sensitive background details or other individuals before uploading

briefs.headline: Government, private medical colleges to adopt health centres across Karnataka
briefs.bodyText:
To strengthen specialist healthcare services at the grassroots level, the State government has asked public and private medical colleges in Karnataka to adopt taluk hospitals, community health centres, and primary health centres.
The Health and Medical Education departments have issued a joint circular to this effect as part of the Chief Minister’s 100-day programme.
Under the initiative, every government and private medical college will adopt one taluk hospital, one community health centre and one primary health centre and provide specialist medical services, training, quality improvement and other healthcare support, according to the circular.
The health centres to be adopted will be identified district-wise. The heads of medical colleges and district health officers will enter into agreements to provide the services.
Specialist care closer to patients
The initiative is expected to improve the availability of specialist doctors at the taluk and community health centre levels, reducing the need for patients to travel to district hospitals or medical colleges for treatment.
The departments said the arrangement would help strengthen treatment for chronic diseases as well as surgical services at the secondary-care level.
The medical colleges will provide the specialist services and other support required by the adopted facilities, with the aim of improving the quality and availability of care closer to where people live.

stories.headline: HDFC Bank sends names of 2 CEO candidates to RBI
stories.deck: HDFC Bank has presented two candidates to the RBI for the upcoming role of managing director and CEO. The board has also sanctioned the promotion of Jimmy Tata to executive director while seeking an extension for V Srinivasa Rangan. This move will elevate the count of whole-time directors to four, enhancing oversight across its subsidiaries. Final approval for these transitions now lies with the…
stories.bodyText:
MUMBAI: HDFC Bank has submitted two names in order of preference to RBI for appointment as its next managing director and CEO, setting in motion the succession process ahead of Sashidhar Jagdishan's exit at the end of Oct.
Alongside the CEO shortlist, the board also approved a revamp of its senior management by elevating chief credit officer Jimmy Tata as an executive director for three years, subject to RBI approval, seeking a one-year extension for executive director V Srinivasa Rangan from Nov 23, 2026, and creating an additional executive director post. The changes will take the number of whole-time directors at India's largest private lender to four. The new position will be finalised in consultation with the incoming MD and CEO.
Expanded board to strengthen oversight of bank's subsidiaries
The expanded board is also expected to strengthen oversight of the bank's subsidiaries, including HDFC Life, HDFC AMC and HDFC ERGO.
"The period of uncertainty is over. The bank has sought to resolve all the issues that it had faced in recent months and with a new CEO in place it is poised to be back on rail," said a person familiar with the matter. 
From getting a new chairman in former CEC Rajiv Kumar to dealing with the charges of mis-selling of bonds as well as addressing the problems around deposits mobilised from a Maharashtra PSU, the board has been addressing the concerns one by one.
HDFC Bank shares (ADS) closed 6.9% higher on NYSE Friday.
The succession process began after Jagdishan decided not to seek another term when his current tenure ends in Oct 2026. Deputy managing director Kaizad M Bharucha is widely seen as a leading internal contender. Bharucha joined HDFC Bank in 1995 and its board in 2014. He has handled corporate banking, wholesale credit, retail assets and the mortgage business.
Names discussed in financial circles have included former SBI chairman Dinesh Khara, Citi India head K Balasubramanian, ICICI Prudential Life CEO Anup Bagchi and former HDFC Bank DMD Paresh Sukthankar.
HDFC Bank
The board changes also strengthen the bank's internal succession bench as it completes the integration following its merger with HDFC Ltd. Tata's elevation adds a senior credit and risk-management executive to the whole-time directorate.
Rangan's proposed extension would provide continuity in real estate finance, treasury and capital management. He joined HDFC Bank's board in Nov 2023 after serving as executive director and CFO of the erstwhile HDFC Ltd. A CA and housing finance veteran, he also represents the bank on the board of HDFC AMC.
The CEO shortlist and the proposed ED appointments now await RBI approval.

stories.headline: Sebi for changes to CAS timing, derivatives settlement prices
stories.deck: Sebi has put forth new proposals aimed at modifying the Closing Auction Session timings and derivatives pricing. Following the recent launch of the session, traders have noted an uptick in market volatility. The regulator is evaluating two potential options for determining derivative settlement prices, suggesting a shift in market timings to include a transition break and longer trading…
stories.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Markets regulator Sebi on Saturday proposed to make some changes to the recently introduced Closing Auction Session's (CAS) timings and to the derivatives pricing mechanism. Launched on Aug 3, CAS had created controversy in the market with traders and investors pointing out that it increased volatility in stock prices and index values.
Last week, Sebi had said that it was working on a consultation paper on CAS and derivatives pricing. The Sebi consultation paper acknowledged that there were some issues relating to pricing of derivatives contracts, especially on days those contracts were expiring.
Among the proposals in Sebi's consultation paper are two choices for arriving at the settlement price for derivatives trades. For one, use a combination of price discovered during the last 30 minutes of regular trading (also called continuous trading session with volume weighted average price or CTS VWAP) and the price discovered during CAS. The second option is to use the price discovered during the last 30 minutes of regular trading and consider CAS trades for derivatives pricing after a year.
The regulator is also proposing changes to market timings. After regular trading ends, there will be a one-minute transition break after which trading will shift to CAS for nine minutes. After that there would be five-minute additional derivatives trading window.
Here under the first option regular trading would continue till 3.30pm. After that there would be CAS and derivatives trading till 3.45pm. Second option is to end regular trading at 3.15pm, followed by CAS and derivatives trading till 3.30pm.
The consultation paper also proposed that the reference price for CAS will continue to be based on the last 15-minute VWAP of continuous trading. It also said that CAS price band would remain at ±3%. It also said orders that are within the ±1% band can be cancelled. On the other hand, orders between ±1% and ±3% cannot be cancelled and can only be modified to improve the price, it said.
The paper proposed that indicative index value will not be disseminated during CAS.
Sebi has asked for comments on the paper till Oct 3.

stories.headline: Senior living market can grow into a $10.1 bn prospect: ASLI-JLL
stories.deck: The addressable market of urban, financially independent senior households in India is expected to grow from 1.7 million in 2026 to 2.1 million by 2030
stories.bodyText:
India’s senior living market is expected to become a $ 10.1 billion opportunity by 2030, requiring $ 7.7 billion capital investment to meet new supply under a policy-driven scenario, according to a ASLI-JLL report “India’s Silver Economy: From Niche to Necessity”.
“With over 166 million Indians aged above 60 and the number projected to double by 2050, there is a need to build an ecosystem of senior citizens. The organised senior living facility penetration is just 1.5%. The opportunity is about building a strong, accessible, and trusted senior care ecosystem,” G. Rajagopal, chairman of the Association of Senior Living India (ASLI), said in a press release.
The addressable market of urban, financially independent senior households in India is expected to grow from 1.7 million in 2026 to 2.1 million by 2030. The opportunity is not just in senior living friendly properties and communities but includes assisted care, healthcare, specialised care, rehabilitation, and other supporting services, says the report.
The organised senior living sector reached 25,050 dwelling units as of June 2026 (at 1.5 %) compared with 6-7 % in the U.S. and 14-15% in New Zealand. The sector registered 14.2 % CAGR between 2024 and first half of 2026.
“We are looking at a market that could scale from 25,050 units to 74,000 units by 2030, unlocking $ 7.7 billion in capital deployment. But the real story is not just independent living, it is the assisted living crisis. We have barely 2,100 assisted living beds today against a projected need of 11,000 by 2030, while the population of 75 plus years is growing at 7.8% annually,” said Karan Singh Sodi, Senior Managing Director, JLL.
However, despite 80 % – 85% occupancy at well-managed facilities, skilled caregiver shortages and high real estate costs remain key constraints. Affordability is a critical barrier, according to the report.
Rental and service-led models are likely to gain significant traction in the coming years, with rental models expected to overtake outright sales. Financial innovations such as repositioned Reverse Mortgage Loans and insurance-linked products could help convert existing assets into viable funding mechanisms for senior care.
The Maharashtra Housing Policy 2025 has formally recognised senior housing through dedicated planning standards and healthcare linkages, while Haryana’s policy combines licensing clarity with Floor Area Ratio incentives to improve project feasibility. Such policy measures can take the market penetration to nearly 2.4 % within four years.
Operators are also investing in digital health infrastructure, including electronic health records, monitoring wearables and telemedicine, alongside quality and accreditation frameworks, the report said.

stories.headline: A roof overhead and then, some
stories.deck: A new service industry has come up across manufacturing corridors in the country, including in Sriperumbudur, seeking to build a business around accommodation for workers and related services, even as large employers continue to rely on in-house and mixed arrangements. This report records this trend and asks if it is here to stay and if it truly benefits factory workers
stories.bodyText:
Sriperumbudur comes alive after 7 p.m. Fast-food carts light up, groups of migrant workers stream out of factory gates towards their accommodation or to dinner, and narrow lanes fill with activity in a town built around manufacturing. There is a sense of relief on the faces after the toil of a full day. Tucked between the automobile and electronics plants that have made this Tamil Nadu industrial corridor famous are three- and four-storey buildings housing paying-guest accommodation for men and women. Many of these buildings have been put up by local landlords to meet the demand from workers who want to live close to their workplaces. Each resident pays a minimum of ₹2,000 a month to share space with at least four other people.
‘Earn and learn’
However, Ramesh (name changed), a 23-year-old from Bhopal, does not have to worry much about this. He arrived in Sriperumbudur a year and a half ago after his elder brother told him about an “earn and learn” programme at a multinational manufacturing company. The four-year programme starts with a monthly pay of around ₹10,000. About ₹1,000 is deducted for food and transport and another ₹1,000 goes into a recurring deposit scheme, he said.
Over the four years, Ramesh will work in several departments of the company. He expects to be offered a job at the end of the programme. His goal is what workers on the programme call “4+2”. That means four years of training, followed by two years of work experience, after which he hopes to leave with a diploma and an experience certificate. For Ramesh, there is one less thing to worry about while he is in Sriperumbudur. He does not have to find a place to stay in a town where Hindi is not widely spoken. The company provides him accommodation.
Karan Chauhan (name changed), 19, joined the same programme at the same company about two months ago. He was sent by his family in Mumbai after personal circumstances forced him to quit a diploma course. Like Ramesh, he is among the young migrants who have come to Sriperumbudur for work and training. For them, the industrial corridor offers a job, accommodation, and the possibility of a better future.
Well-managed services
It is this growing migrant workforce, ranging from young trainees to experienced factory workers, that a small group of companies is now seeking to serve through professionally managed accommodation and other services.
In accommodation units run by professional operators, there are bunk beds, some space to play indoor games, food arrangements, spacious rooms, and facilities for yoga. Records of residents are maintained, adding another layer of organisation to what is otherwise a largely informal housing market around the industrial corridor.
Companies have traditionally used a mix of in-house accommodation, rented rooms, and private hostels to house workers around industrial clusters. Now, companies such as Nia and Manzl are building businesses around the same requirement. Nia describes itself as something broader than a housing provider. “We are labour infrastructure with a roof, not housing with jobs attached,” the company said in written responses to questions from The Hindu. Its model combines managed living with work continuity and everyday essentials such as meals and groceries and telehealth.
Wide client base
Nia said it currently operates across four industrial corridors (NCR, Chakan in Pune, Bengaluru, and Sriperumbudur) and serves more than 10,000 members. Its client base spans automotive, electronics, manufacturing, logistics, and IT services. Manzl, which operates in Tada and Sri City and has identified a location at Oragadam, describes itself as an industrial housing platform. Its business covers construction, facility management, and a digital worker management platform. It provides accommodation ranging from dormitory-style housing for shop-floor workers to corporate housing for white-collar employees.
Both companies say living conditions can affect whether or not workers remain with an employer.
Nia describes worker infrastructure as “a strategic lever on retention and output”. Manzl co-founder Rohit George said the demand is being driven by the location of new manufacturing plants and the scale of hiring. He pointed to industrial clusters such as Sriperumbudur-Oragadam, Sanand (Gujarat), Chakan (Maharashtra), and Narasapura (Karnataka), where plants are being built, away from established housing markets. He said some clients who previously rented rooms from local landlords, operated their own hostels, and separately arranged food, housekeeping and security, are now looking to hand the entire function to a single provider.
“Today a client hands over the whole thing to one provider. The building, the services therein, and the reporting layer on top,” he said. “The shift is from procuring rooms to outsourcing a function.”
The services being sought now go beyond accommodation, according to Manzl. They include food, housekeeping, security, utilities, transport, connectivity, and recreation. Its technology platform also provides employers with information on occupancy and rostering, along with onboarding, offboarding, and a multilingual helpdesk for residents.
Manzl said electronics and semiconductors are seeing the fastest adoption, followed by automotive and components. It expects textiles to see more outsourcing of accommodation too, given its large factory workforce and historical reliance on in-house hostels.
The pitch to employers is partly built around retention. Nia said its internal cohort-based tracking shows worker retention rising from around 53% to about 70% among members on professionally managed living, measured through Day-30 retention. The company also stresses that better accommodation is not a substitute for better wages. “Infrastructure complements better wages. It doesn’t compensate for lower ones,” Nia said.
Secure housing
The company’s model differs from conventional employer accommodation in another way. Nia says workers do not automatically lose their accommodation if they leave their employer. A worker can continue living in a Nest while looking for another job. The membership can shift from an employer-linked arrangement to a direct one until the worker is placed again. “Losing a job shouldn’t mean losing your home too, especially for a migrant worker far from family,” the company said.
Elevar Equity, which has invested in Nia, sees the model as part of a wider formalisation of the ecosystem around migrant workers.
Managing partner of the firm Jyotsna Krishnan said workers often migrate to industrial centres with specific savings goals. Poor housing, food, and other services can eat into those earnings.
Emerging category
Elevar describes “comprehensive worker infrastructure” as an emerging category. It sees an opportunity to formalise the existing ecosystem of unorganised hostels and fragmented services rather than simply replace it. It also sees a change in how companies view worker attrition. The investor said the problem is increasingly being viewed not only as a recruitment or wage issue but also as an infrastructure issue. But the shift is not widespread yet.
An executive of a large manufacturing company, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the company maintains its own systems for housing and managing workers and does not currently use external operators of this kind.
Very large companies generally do not opt for such arrangements because their requirements around scale, specifications, and control are different, the executive said. The company could consider external arrangements if need be, but is not doing so at present.
A second executive from another large manufacturer said the company uses a mix of internal and external arrangements. The executive also stressed the importance of organisations caring for contract and migrant workers in a manner comparable to their direct employees.
That suggests the emerging market for specialised accommodation operators is not yet replacing employer-run housing across the manufacturing sector. Different companies are using different models based on their requirements.
The emergence of these companies comes as the government looks at worker accommodation as part of the infrastructure needed for manufacturing. The Union Budget 2024-25 proposed rental housing with dormitory-style accommodation for industrial workers through a public-private partnership model, with viability-gap funding and commitments from anchor industries.
NITI Aayog’s December 2024 report on ‘Site Adjacent Factory Employee Accommodation’ recommended a market-driven model for long-term dormitory-style accommodation near workplaces. It envisages private developers playing a role in developing and operating such housing, with government support including viability-gap funding. The report said such accommodation could facilitate labour mobility, improve productivity, and worker welfare and retention. It also recommended treating workers’ accommodation as critical infrastructure for India’s manufacturing growth.
Only complementary
For Nia, the role of private operators is complementary to the existing welfare systems rather than a replacement for them. The company said it operates alongside schemes such as One Nation One Ration One Card, ESIC, EPFO, and e-Shram.
Nia also distinguishes its role from the employer’s statutory responsibilities. It said its role is to execute the legally required floor around accommodation and welfare and then provide services beyond those minimum requirements.
For Ramesh and Karan, much of this distinction is not visible. What matters to them is the job, the room, and the opportunity to build a future away from home.

briefs.headline: How sanctioned ships are heading to Alang for recycling
briefs.bodyText:
During its blockade of Venezuela in December of last year, the U.S. government sought to seize several tankers that were calling on Venezuela. Among them was Marinera, which the U.S. pursued for nearly a month and seized off Iceland, and Lileo. In August, the U.S. government sold the two vessels to GMS, a leading buyer of vessels going for demolition, which has brought them to Alang in Gujarat for recycling.
Marinera and Lileo are among the more than thousand vessels sanctioned by the U.S. While these two were directly sold by the U.S. government, many sanctioned ships owned by sanctioned entities have been coming to Alang for recycling in recent months. For instance, Lloyd’s List reported on Sept. 4 that the Double In, a Very Large Gas Carrier that had been sanctioned by the U.S. for dealing in Iranian cargoes, had beached in Alang for recycling after ownership was transferred to a shell company.
It would seem that beyond just the age of the vessel, the renewed focus on such ships due to the West Asia crisis has made operating some of these ships more challenging. For instance, eight sanctioned ships identified by Lloyds List had identified as having scrapped in January and February this year, four were built well into the 2000s, which means they were not quite old enough for demolition. Blockades, interdiction of these vessels in the seas, and choking of demand are contributing to this trend, say industry sources.
“Bangladesh, which is the leading ship recycling nation in the world, as well as Pakistan, are not accepting sanctioned ships for recycling, so India is becoming the major destination for sanctioned vessel recycling,” says Anil Sharma, founder and CEO of GMS. Companies such as GMS purchase the vessel, prepare it for recycling, and bring it to the recycling yard to which they have sold the vessel.
Sanctions by the U.S. will lock the ship owner and related firms out of the mainstream global financial system. Indian banks and financial firms will therefore not accept transactions involving these entities. Industry sources say that there is typically an Indian firm in the chain so the immediate transactions of recycling are conducted in rupees but eventually the money could be routed through other channels such as the Hong Kong dollar, digital-crypto currencies, and rupee-rouble exchanges to the firms sanctioned by the U.S.
But the U.S. and other sanctioning entities are not entirely averse to scrapping of the ships they have sanctioned. They see it as a route to put the ships out of business. A U.S. treasury department official, for instance, wrote in an email to The Hindu: “To protect maritime safety, we are committed to responsible solutions to get sanctioned vessels off the water. We consider these matters on a case-by-case basis.” The European Union is considering such case-by-case approvals of demolitions of ships dealing with Russian oil it has sanctioned.
The U.S. government has put together a process for approving such demolitions for recycling. “The U.S. government may approve such demolitions if the money was going towards funding what the U.S. government had a problem with in the first place. For instance, it may approve if the money was going to repay a loan taken from a non-sanctioned bank before the sanctions or if it would go to paying unpaid crew wages and so on,” adds Mr. Sharma.
GMS has acquired six approvals from the U.S. government. The first approval took seven months while the following ones were quicker.
Indian regulations
India’s Recycling of Ships Regulations 2026 primarily updates the regulations on compliance with recent international rules such as the Hong Kong Convention. It does not specifically address the issue of ships sanctioned by the U.S. and EU. Officially, the Indian government does not recognize these sanctions and recognizes only those by the United Nations. Nevertheless, the regulations do talk about scrutinizing the documents submitted by the ship owner by the Director General of Maritime Affairs for authenticity to clamp down on fraud.
For Alang, the competent authority to handle the ships is the Gujarat Maritime Board. The 2026 regulations specify that the ship recycler shall submit to the authority the originals of: Certificate of Registry; valid third-party/oil-pollution insurance certificate; certificates of competency for master/officers/ratings; Inventory of Hazardous Materials (IHM) certificate and/or Ready for Recycling Certificate among other documents.
If any of the documents submitted is found to be unreliable, or if a submitted document is found to be fake or conceals a material fact, the shipowner shall not be given permission to anchor, enter, beach, or begin cutting, as per the regulations. Sanctioned ships often sail without proper insurance such as P&I or the IHM certificate. And India’s regulations specifically talk about insurance covering “third-party liability, oil pollution damage, and wreck removal” and the IHM certificate

briefs.headline: SEBI proposes to tweak CAS after industry feedback
briefs.deck: The proposals are aimed at addressing concerns emerging from the initial implementation of the CAS and ensuring a more orderly and transparent expiry-day trading and settlement process.
briefs.bodyText:
The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) has proposed to review expiry-day settlement prices, market timings, order handling and information dissemination under the newly introduced Closing Auction Session (CAS), following industry feedback on initial operational snags.
In a consultation paper released on September 12, SEBI said the existing methodology for determining expiry-day settlement prices for index and stock derivatives needs to be reviewed amid heightened activity in expiring index options and derivatives trading based on the Indicative Equilibrium Price (IEP) during the CAS.
“In view of the hyperactivity in expiring index options contracts along with IEP based derivatives trading during CAS, it is proposed to review the existing methodology for determining the settlement price of both index and stock derivatives contracts on the expiry day,” market regulator said.
The regulator has proposed two alternatives for determining expiry-day settlement prices. The first involves using a blended volume-weighted average price (VWAP), while the second would temporarily revert to the pre-CAS settlement-price mechanism for expiry days before transitioning to the blended VWAP methodology.
SEBI has proposed discontinuing the display of indicative index value, while continuing to provide the IEP for individual securities.
According to the regulator, displaying the indicative index value could lead to its misinterpretation by market participants and potentially influence trading and position-taking during the auction session.
The proposed changes also include adjustments to closing market timings for stocks and the futures and options (F&O) segment, along with other modifications to the functioning of the CAS.
